bramfatura.Shartamakhum.desc:
The bramfatura of Mercury, revealed through telefaturic dislocation, is a land of sand and molten stone, all woven from heat. The sunlight here has weight. It presses down on shoulders and spines, grinding the bones. Even the dunes whisper underfoot, their glassy skin rustling like a tired breath.

The Farises—wandering knights of the desert—drift through the endless, broken wasteland with their Malāks at their side. They hunt each other endlessly, each duel meant to turn an enemy into an abd. These skirmishes have lasted for as long as the Solar System itself. To write the history of Shartmakhum would be like tracing the quarrels of lion prides in Africa—a pack rises, fights to survive, clashes with others, then falls apart. It happens again and again, across ages of stone and dust. Yet for the Farises, every slight, no matter how old, weighs heavy. Faris Zauba was once enslaved, forced to serve his captor for millennia. He won back his title, took revenge, and became lord of his own band. Now the fallen Maimun as-Sahabi wanders Shartmakhum, driven by the need to destroy the one who stepped out of his shadow and became his punishment.

The coming of humankind to Mercury broke the old balance of war. A new source of gavvakh had appeared, strong enough to end the endless, senseless dance of hatred. Once, the greatest triumph was to turn a foe into an abd, or, in the rarest cases, to melt him down into a Malāk. Now, with enough gavvakh, a Faris could erase an enemy completely—cast him into true oblivion. And so the sultans of Shartmakhum turned their gaze from the blinding Sun and began to gather their scattered bands. Whoever raises an army first will be the first to reach the place where violence in the material world begins to boil.

There are few humans on Mercury. Shartmakhum trembles but never storms. It shifts and reshapes itself with frightening speed, yet its voice is calm—more a Sufi's meditation than a dervish's whirl.

High above it all lies Fukabirna, a silent ocean of molten infra-iron. The sultans feel a searing pain whenever they withhold the gathered gavvakh from their master. That pain moves through the dunes like sound through a drum, a deep pulse under the sand. The Faris-mujtahids read these tremors as signs of loyalty to the Red and Gold Throne, and take Fukabirna's silence as readiness to meet Gagtungr when he reveals his faces. To offer a tribute worthy of him, Shartmakhum strains itself to the limit.

Here, even light carries weight, and memories do too. Every step grinds against the glass of old vows. Every breath tastes of hot copper and the names of the true lord of fire.

bramfatura.Ur_Awakened.desc:
The telefaturic dislocation reveals Ur as a steppe of red dust and basalt plateaus, where ziggurats the color of dried blood rise against the horizon. Winds carve the landscape as cuneiform cuts into wet clay. Along the dry riverbeds lie channels hardened with ancient blood, and every step of every ziggurat beats like a drum of war.

The lord of the bramfatura of Mars is Lugal Urparp. When Gagtungr vanished, he raised his title above all others and proclaimed himself Emperor of the Solar System. The alliance of Fokerma and Tezctlan subdued him. For the Solar System, the ziggurats of Ur fell silent, and the wells were sealed.

Now, awakened, Urparp does not repeat his old mistakes. He and the army he leads are fervent servants of the Red and Gold Throne. While Urparp was weighed down by physical matter and imprisoned in the world of humans, he learned how to linger within it. Moreover, from his captivity emerged Shedu's Thousand along with him—an army of ritual warriors bound by passion, recruited from those possessed by war. This army operates within the physical realm. Their vows to kill and to die are inscribed in cuneiform upon metal and flesh. The obelisk-cairns they erect serve as anchors for quasimorph flesh, stitching battlefields to cosmic and planetary stations so that war can never depart from them.

Ur swears to purge the world of impostors and new rebels before the return of the solar lord. Urparp's hatred for Tezctlan is cold and exact. He sees the Emerald Empire as a mirror of his own downfall. The law of Ur is brief: there is no cowardice, no substitution of judgment with mercy. On the steps of the ziggurats lie skulls—garlands of trophies marking uncomplicated oaths fulfilled.

The impulses of Ur, when sunlight reached Earth through Mars, gave humankind more than landscapes and nature. The wheel, bronze, the written word, and the rule of law—all were born from the deep strata of the Martian bramfatura. Even when Ur was sealed, weighed down by the body of its lord, its rhythms seeped through to Earth—in marching steps, in the iron discipline of assembly lines, in the rhythmic clatter of the first combat vehicles' tracks, in the habit of forcing the defeated to sign beneath the text of surrender.

Listen closely to the echo of footsteps on basalt, and you can hear the formula by which Urparp answers the challenges of the universe: "Command — and they shall obey."
